claim: Treat mixdown as its own stage: start from clean raw audio files (including MIDI bounced to audio) in a fresh project, even for your own productions.
Rest 10 days or so away from a song you also recorded before mixing it, for objectivity.
Prep order: label and colour tracks, add section markers, fix grid or sync problems, listen to each track alone, cut silences, fix noises and clicks, mark special moments, then mult.
Mult (split to separate tracks) sections that need different processing, such as verse and chorus vocals, sparse and dense sections, or rimshot and normal snare.
Timing and tuning fixes come before balancing and processing.
Timing edit order: choose the one part with the best groove (usually drums), fix it, then add bass, then other rhythm parts, one at a time.
For layered parts (doubled guitars, stacked backing vocals), tighten each layer alone, then combine.
Low-end plan for the mix: high-pass every track, strip low end from secondary parts, keep real sub energy on as few tracks as possible.
Late in the mix, check on several monitoring systems and at several volumes, take breaks, and avoid finalizing late in the day.
Finish by printing alternate versions (vocal up, bass up, vocal out, instrumental, a capella, stems).
Room modes: first mode is about 172 divided by the distance in metres between parallel surfaces. Later modes are multiples of it. A 2.42 m ceiling gives about 71, 142, 213 Hz.
A single room mode can move the heard level by about 20 dB.
Typical bass guitar lowest fundamental is about 41 Hz. Pianos, organs and synths go into the 20 to 40 Hz bottom octave.

Ported small monitors: response is flat to about 55 Hz and then drops steeply. Port-blocked, the response leaves the window near 100 Hz. A 30 Hz kick can sit about 12 dB lower than a 50 Hz kick on such speakers, so mixers boost it too much.
Mid-range crossover in cheap two-way monitors is around 2 to 3 kHz, where combing hurts most.
Small playback devices give little output below about 200 Hz.
Bottom octave (about 40 Hz and down) is vital for club music and needs a full-range system.
Mineral-fibre traps get weak below about 100 Hz.

Pro practice: little exists below 120 to 150 Hz apart from kick and bass, so high-pass nearly everything else. Another engineer says secondary tracks can lose low content up to about 160 Hz and the mix still sounds big.
Boundary effect: speakers against a wall boost bass by up to 3 dB, in a corner up to 6 dB.
Mids matter most: the mid region carries the main information and survives every playback system.
Subsonic sources: bass guitar harmonics, vocal plosives (p, b, w), mic draughts and stand rumble, sampled snares cut from full mixes, DC offset.
DC offset shifts the waveform, raises peaks and adds no loudness.
Subsonic kick content can eat about 3 dB of mix headroom with no audible change (demo file).
Sibilance and vocal air can be pushed too far; one named reference is an example of that extreme.
Top end: loud monitoring exaggerates harshness. Quiet listening needs more high-frequency enhancement to keep clarity at home, in cars and in offices.
Hearing fatigue dulls high-frequency sensitivity first.
Too much bass makes the apparent vocal level seem to drop about 3 dB each kick hit, and the mix sounds quieter on radio.
Loudness-matching references to the mix is essential, because louder sounds better.
Super-loud masters hide mix balance. Workarounds: use unmastered or lightly mastered references, or apply loudness processing to your mix when comparing.
Master-buss compression can be recorded off and on versions. Buss compression on instrumentals, a cappellas or stems stops them summing back to the full mix.
Metering: use both average and peak readings, and watch each track for level irregularities.
Keep the loudness trade-off in mind: loudness enhancement has side effects, so decide the trade consciously.
Mono summing makes centre sounds about 3 dB louder relative to side sounds.
Check mono compatibility: spaced-mic recordings (drums, room, ensembles, piano) comb-filter in mono. Simulated stereo reverbs and delays can too.
Out-of-polarity stereo content cancels in mono. Synth patches and stereo wideners that invert one side can lose hook lines.
Many systems are effectively mono or poorly stereo: phone hold, club PAs, shop PAs, FM radio on weak signal, bars, car (driver sits off-centre), laptops, TVs. So the mono check stays essential.
Headphones widen the image to about 180 degrees versus about 60 for speakers. Hard-panned parts feel detached. Lead parts can end up balanced too low and delay/reverb too loud.
Tightly timed doubles panned opposite sides need extra precision because the ear is sensitive to timing gaps between similar sounds in different positions.
Left-right images are firmer than centre phantom images, so judge central balances in mono.
Cut low end from secondary instruments so only bass and kick own the sub range.
Option: split the sub-100 Hz range of the bass for separate processing and metering, or replace it with a dedicated sub synth part.
Kick low-end lag: a sub that arrives late after the attack sounds less punchy.
Bass synths with an overblown fundamental may wander below audibility.
Mono low-end check: concentrated low end on few tracks makes mastering fixes easier.
Judge exact balances from a single small speaker in mono, where centre and edge items are equally stable.
Lead vocal level is the most common revision, so print vocal-up (and optionally other vocal-level) versions. Spike Stent notes labels want the vocal very loud but the track needs power.
Bass level also gets revisited; print bass up, bass and kick up, or kick up versions.
Intelligibility acid test: two small cheap speakers side by side (near-mono, no gain from centre summing); if lyrics and melody read, they will survive.
Too loud bass lowers the mix's apparent loudness on radio.
Different monitor levels reveal different issues: quiet shows whether key elements are loud enough, loud shows harshness, impact and low end.
If you do not want to turn the monitors down, the mix may need more work.
A mix that feels powerful when quiet will stay powerful when loud.
Genre example: bright for a pop singer, less top end on a rap vocal.
Compare to commercial references, matched in loudness, using fast switching. Short highlight snippets show contrast best.
Use uncompressed (WAV) references. Lossy files and streams make an easier target.
Choose references for sonics, not for song taste. Check each on several systems. Pick the best-sounding track by an engineer, not always the hit.
Match references to genre and era: tonality, compression and reverb use all vary.
Use different references for different jobs (bass, vocal, reverb, buss processing). Add end-stop references for too much top end, low end or vocal air.
Do not copy; use references for inspiration and competitiveness.
Reference in a separate project so you cannot instantly tweak. This forces a considered judgment.
Reference tracks also test unfamiliar rooms; judge them before your ears adapt (about four days).
Monitoring set: full-range nearfields (spend most, active, unported if budget is under about 1500 GBP), single mono small speaker, headphones, one grotbox.
Budget guide: treatment spend about equal to speakers; about a dozen 10 cm slabs of mineral fibre; about 4 to 5 square metres of 10 cm foam.
Do not use EQ or room-correction to fix room modes. Broad tone tweaks only.
Speakers: equal distances to the listener, tweeter near ear height, polarity check, err on narrower spacing, vertical orientation.
Switch monitors often to reset your ear; take breaks (e.g. 20 minutes on, 20 off in dense songs).
Never finalize a mix late in the day; sleep on it. Do not monitor loudly for long; do loud checks only briefly.
Calibrated monitor level is optional; loudness-matched referencing is more reliable.
Loudness perception: more extremes heard when loud, mids dominate when quiet. About 60 dB change gives a noticeable tone shift.
Averaging the room: listen in several spots and from another room; use a high-resolution spectrum analyser to check octave balance in the low end.
Watching woofer cone movement can reveal subsonic trouble but should not guide balance.
Referencing against low-quality or favourite-from-memory tracks.
Judging bass on ported or untreated-room monitors without a cross-check.
Boosting a low kick because the monitors recess that range.
Covering the whole room in thin foam; deadens highs and leaves bass untouched.
Pulling speakers too far apart, sitting off-axis, or having wrong polarity.
Trusting only stereo; leaving out-of-polarity synth content and spaced-mic combing unchecked.
Leaving subsonic rubbish, rumble or DC in tracks.
Too much low end on many instruments, which blocks headroom.
Mixing late at night; one case mixed huge drums and bass, then lost the song by morning.
Running MIDI live during mixing instead of bouncing.
Trying to fix timing by editing many single hits when whole sections need sliding.
Judging timing from the grid rather than by ear; need two bars of run-up when auditioning.
Lead-vocal timing blind spot in otherwise tight tracks.
Leaving master-buss processing on stems or instrumentals.
Loud monitoring makes a weak mix feel strong.
Pro engineers often work at low volume; Allen Sides listens loud for 20 to 30 seconds only.
Comb filtering: delays under about 25 ms colour tone; longer delays are heard as echoes. A 0.5 ms delay cancels 1 kHz and keeps 2 kHz in phase.
Room reflections from beyond about 3 m matter less in small rooms.
Mix recall is unreliable; printed alternates are safer.
Alternates: vocal up, bass up, vocal out (TV mix), instrumental, a cappella, and stems for drums, bass, guitars, keys, pads, vocals, effects.
Alternates for editing out words; the instrumental plus a cappella can rescue vocal level mistakes.
Edit crossfade lengths: about 2 ms in noisy spots, about 5 ms before a percussive attack, 50 ms under heavy chorus masking, over 100 ms to blend long edits.
Matched-waveform edits suit long held notes (m, n sounds); vibrato makes them hard.
Time-stretch is a last resort for polyphonic or noisy material because of artifacts.
Live parts mixed with machine parts need tight sync to avoid phase issues.
Track counts and layouts: pros standardise layouts and often limit counts; submix to fewer channels.
Do not obsess over pitch or timing purity: serve the music. Classical solo piano tolerates no artifacts; a background pop vocal tolerates them.
Mix in order of importance: sections first (most important chorus first), then instruments within each section
Mix the biggest chorus first, then step the other sections down so each later climax stays biggest
If a midsection pushed too far makes the next chorus feel like a letdown, reduce the midsection, not the chorus
Mix the intro last if the song builds from it, but the intro still has to grab the listener
Start with the most sonically important instrument, not just the musical one (for example bass or drums in a riff-led track)
Build the balance by adding one instrument at a time, each less important than the last
Vocal share of production time can exceed half
Kick, bass and synth hooks may deserve most of the time
Spend time on what carries the commercial hook; spend little on low-value detail
Filter most tracks with a high-pass; low-pass is rarely needed
Slopes of 6, 12 or 18 dB/octave for cleanup; avoid steeper slopes and resonant HPFs
Set HPF cutoff by raising it until the low end changes, then back off about 15%
HPF can soften kick, snare and tom attack before the tone changes, so set it lower on these
Bass: kick HPF example stopped affecting thump at about 42Hz, then set to 35Hz
Bass low end that is too high can make kick sound boxy; sort kick and bass with EQ before adding weight
Low-pass filter only for noisy amp or fizzy DI tracks, and sparingly, to keep "air"
Kick/bass conflict in the low end: carve space for the kick in the bass part (rap wants a crushing kick)
Bass: add top end so it cuts through (chart and rock)
Low midrange of bass is often left free in chart pop; rock/metal put low-mid emphasis on guitars
Narrow notches on drum resonances; find them with a high-resolution spectrum analyzer
Mains hum notching: 50Hz (or 60Hz) and its harmonics
Wide Q for most EQ work; narrow boosts take the music out of an instrument
Bass length: 20 to 30Hz changes perceived note length; cut there for tighter bass
Kick and bass tuning: think in bands, not single frequencies
Masking example: cymbals above 5kHz hide the vocal top end
Balance EQ first, tone EQ second
Compressor threshold: start with at least 6dB of gain reduction on peaks, then adjust make-up gain
Make-up gain: set it manually rather than automatically
Ratio guide: about 2:1 for guitar, about 3:1 or lower for balance fixes, high ratio (12:1 or more, up to infinity:1) for spike control
Use the lowest ratio that solves the problem; high ratio flattens performance
Limiter: high-ratio compressor; check output level after it
Chain compressors in series: each does a small job instead of one doing a big one
Attack under about 50ms can cut kick bass content (phase/shape change)
Fast attack and fast release: less transient (less snap)
Fast attack and slow release: more consistent hit level
Slow attack and slow release: less sustain, transient gets through
Fast attack and release on bass or fine acoustic material can cause waveform distortion
Gentle compression with soft-knee 2:1 or 3:1 for a first layer on lead vocal
Vocal: use a faster, higher-ratio layer after the first if peaks still poke out
Parallel compression: blend heavy compressed and dry signal; judge the blend, not the compressed track on its own
Parallel and dry tracks: balance on a group fader so the loudness bias does not decide the blend
Expander threshold: signals below threshold get reduced; 1:1 means none, 4:1 is strong
Gate chatter: add a few ms of hold time or hysteresis
Expander before compressor in the chain for most cases
Range control on a gate: set max reduction to remove spill, then reduce it to taste
Threshold-independent transient shaping: adjust attack and sustain without a threshold
Lookahead: a few ms helps percussive gates keep the transient
Tempo-synced gating or tremolo: shape level on the beat grid (for example off-beat guitar)
Keep kick, snare, bass and solo lead vocal near centre
Bass centred for mono sum and for vinyl safety
Panning to an extreme costs about 3dB of level in mono
Opposition panning: pair similar parts left and right to keep the image balanced
Pan laws: 6dB, 3dB and 4.5dB differ in what changes in mono vs stereo; centre parts gain about 3dB when summed to mono
Pan-law choice matters mainly for automated pan moves
Double-tracked vocals and guitars often opposition-panned
Stereo file: work on both sides through one channel; check polarity and time alignment for mono
Use a channel-swap check to see if a stereo source is truly centred
Vectorscope or swapping L/R shows off-centre sources
Multimic instruments: polarity and phase matching avoid comb filtering; deliberate phase tricks can sculpt tone
Delayed mic of a few ms can change tone a lot at a low level
Stereo overhead vs close snare: time-alignment changes the first-arrival image
Time-aligned close mics: transients sharper, close mics pull images toward the listener (taste)
Delaying close mics 5 to 10ms more than simple alignment can soften movement-based tone changes
First track: set a safe level; leave headroom so the master does not clip
Floating-point mixing: meters may read high without damage; keep 24dB or more channel headroom where practical
Keep the fader near unity (0dB) and use gain plugins for big changes
Fader stability test: if the level feels unstable, the track needs processing
Fader problems map to fixes: kick too quiet means a separate kick fader or multing; chord level swing means dynamics; boomy resonance means EQ
Level test: a 0.1 to 0.2dB change should be audible when the mix is close to right
Lead vocal: should sound slightly too quiet on loud monitors and slightly too loud on quiet monitors
Balancing with pink noise: noted as a red herring; if used, peak near -15dBFS (book text garbled, check)
Starting balance without processing: leave a track unprocessed if it balances at a static fader level
Drum case: check drum level against the overheads; start from the stronger section first
Compress the balance only when needed (no compression where fader is stable)
Group compression is weaker than per-track compression for keeping a balance between backing voices
Use a secondary, low-fi speaker (Auratone-type) alongside main monitors
Switch monitors often, vary listening levels, take breaks
Reference tracks: use a few early to calibrate ears; detailed referencing at the end
Compare the processed mix against commercial references at the end
Listen in mono as part of checks
EQ presets are of little use: each mix needs its own settings
Judging EQ on the solo button; EQ in context
Boosting makes things louder and biases choices; prefer cuts
More than one filter or more than 6dB of boost on a track is probably too much
Overprocessing (too many plugins, too much compression) costs smoothness
Adding plugins to later tracks: later tracks get more damage because they have less room
Automatic make-up gain hides the real change and encourages overcooking
Trusting meters or pitch graphs over ears (pitch tools and graphs)
Over-tuning or pitch-set-and-forget kills expression
Removing breath noise from lead vocals can make the take feel unnatural
Trying to make every instrument sound best alone is a waste; judge the whole mix
Parallel compression and EQ add loudness; compare at matched level
Too much repetition: a riff repeated more than three times in a row needs a fill
Check that DAW plugin delay compensation is on
Comping: at least three takes per section; eight takes for a pro lead vocal comp
Lead vocal comp: take each phrase from takes that work, then fill gaps
Vocals: feel over pitch perfection; tune for pitch centres, keep vibrato
Tuning: tune the monophonic parts first (bass, lead) and keep noisy guitars alone if possible
Drum tuning to key: tuned drum overtones should fit the track
Tuning: keep correction slow; large shifts done offline first
Crossfades: equal-power for most edits, equal-gain for matched-waveform edits
Hide edits in silence, noise or masked moments
Arrangement: keep three main points of interest at a time, then thin the rest
Fill every few seconds in chart styles; keep something new every four to eight bars
Drop chorus: mute most parts before the final chorus to get a second payoff
Bass line as a second melody
Fades: a fade-down on a subdivision can make the groove feel faster or slower
Shift the groove by a few ms per instrument with a time-offset parameter, not by dragging regions
Use a time-offset parameter so offsets can be undone
Rotate phase in a drum mic to fill the snare low mid and tame a resonance
EQ for distance: duller means further away; reduce top end on background vocals
Consider linear-phase EQ for multimic work; watch for pre-ringing on drums and CPU load
Tonal EQ (after balance is set): use two character EQs, compare them
Build the balance in order of importance; add sweeteners (reverb/delay/stereo) only after raw tracks balance, so you know how much space is left.
Per new track: set pan, filter, polarity/phase, then fader; if the fader will not settle, keep trying processing until it does.
Balance needs come first; tonal "prettying" is judged separately by taste.
Revisiting earlier tracks while adding later ones is normal.
Tonal/sustain reverbs and delays: do them early, during balancing. Blend/size reverbs: after the full balance is set.
Master buss: EQ after buss compression; stereo-width tweak late; buss processing should be in before mix is final, since it changes how channels sit.
Bottom-up (fix per-track phase/balance/masking first, then buss) vs top-down (buss first, fast): author prefers bottom-up with an early buss EQ for tone; top-down can lead to overprocessed busses.
Referencing against commercial tracks comes once the first section is nearly done; do not mix other sections before referencing the first. Quick early reference to catch bad faders is fine.
If tonal or width is clearly off against references, fix with EQ or mid/side straight away, then move that to the master buss.
De-esser goes last in a vocal chain, but before any high-frequency exciter/distortion.
Noise reduction goes first in a track's chain.
Many small tweaks beat a few big moves.
If 5 minutes of EQ has not solved a track, EQ is not the whole answer; add or process differently.
Reverb returns: cut below about 300 Hz (typically a roll-off of low mids around 200-300 Hz) to protect bass headroom and avoid mud. Amount is genre-dependent; verify against references.
Reverb tails on bass instruments are usually counterproductive; high-pass the size reverb return.
Dark (low-passed or high-shelf-cut) reverb returns are less audible as effects; bright returns give away the effect.
808 kick: a little distortion pushes energy into 120-140 Hz and above so it is audible on small speakers.
Gated sine tone for kick weight: start near 50 Hz, tune by ear, keep it in tune with the bass line.
Vocal de-essing: sibilance often upper highs; a second de-esser may work around 2 kHz. Harshness de-ess starts near 2 kHz up to about 3 kHz max.
Singer resonance peaks usually appear above 1 kHz; hardness when singing loud lives around 4-5 kHz; static EQ there dulls quiet sections, so use dynamic EQ.
Reverb/delay low-frequency sub-20 ms delays cause comb filtering; below about 10 ms comb effects are strongest.
An 8 kHz peaking cut in dynamic EQ is one de-ess substitute.
Master-buss EQ: lift above about 10 kHz with one good EQ rather than many cheap channel boosts; digital EQ boosting highs on many channels gets harsh.
Mono-incompatible Sides energy at 5 kHz and 16 kHz (seen in a pop-rap hit) wrecks mono tone.
Keep EQ boost under 6 dB, one band, wide bandwidth; prefer cuts and shelves.
Boosting highs on a source with nothing above ~4 kHz but noise cannot help; add content via distortion instead.
Reverb pre-delay EQ: set the reverb return's low end by ear versus references.
Buss "glue" compression: usually 2 to 3 dB gain reduction at most, slow attack, auto release, ratio under 2:1, even 1.1:1.
Pumping buss compression: may reach 8 dB reduction on peaks, with faster attack/release and higher ratios.
Gentle top-down loudness squeeze: low ratio, low threshold, gain reduction kept within about 3 dB.
Bass ducked by kick for low-end clarity: about 2 dB for a moment.
Keyed ducking of guitars from the vocal: 1 to 2 dB is often plenty.
Compressors react more to lows, less to highs: heavy vocal compression exaggerates sibilance; heavy compression on full-range material gives pumping. A low-shelf cut in the detector reduces pumping.
Pumping can be wanted for power; it also raises average level.
De-esser use: two de-essers working lightly can beat one heavy one.
Distortion lowers dynamic range; clipping can round off spiky percussion.
Sub-synth parts need tight dynamics or they eat headroom; compress the MIDI part and its output.
Do not match loudness by meter peaks: match subjective/integrated loudness (LUFS) when A/B-ing processing.
Loudness target depends on genre: jazz/blues less loud than pop/metal.
Loudness processors' costs: limiting causes pumping, bass distortion, softened transients, quieter-sounding drums. Top-down squeeze boosts low-level detail, reverb, noise; sparse sections get louder.
Multiband compression on the mix buss is best left to mastering.
Multiband: use only the bands needed; each band needs its own attack/release; avoid presets.
Expanding the low band of a kick tightens an up-tempo mix.
Gates on spill: filter the detector, but a high-frequency-dominated attack may open late; use look-ahead.
Side signal is lost in mono; heavy Sides boosts can make parts drop or vanish when summed. Check mono.
Widen less-important parts only; keep key elements (bass, kick, snare, lead) center-focused.
High-pass the Sides signal to fix low-frequency phase problems in mono; "very common" in chart music.
Boosting very high frequencies in Sides widens on good systems and costs little in mono.
Vectorscope shows overall width and lopsidedness but not per-track mono collapse or frequency-specific problems; use a stereo/MS spectrum analyzer for that.
Lower the Middle level of pads and reverb returns to clear center space.
Fake double-tracks by editing repeated sections (not a delayed copy, which phase-cancels in mono); then pan opposite.
Unpitched/pad textures for width rarely hurt mono compatibility.
EQ-based widening: complementary alternating boost/cut on L and R copies; mono-friendly but destabilises the image, use for background parts.
Comb-filter widener: ~20 ms delay, no feedback, polarity invert one channel's return.
Haas delay: echo within about 30 ms; shorter gets worse mono cancellation; image feels lopsided; homogenises and pushes sound back.
Pitch widening: +5 cents one side, -5 cents other; classic pitch-shifted delay patch good for lead vocals; check mono.
Auto-pan for width: low depth, sine/triangle, 5 to 10 Hz rate.
Chorus/flanger/phaser as send with low depth/feedback widen; mono damage softened by modulation.
Delay returns: true-stereo setup best for blend/size; mono-in/mono-out global delays narrow the mix and clutter center; ping-pong balances panned repeats.
Subsynth: use mono patches, avoid detuned layers; remove the original bass fundamental (steep high-pass or notch) to prevent phase cancellation.
Layered kicks/samples: align timing and polarity; wrong polarity costs low-end weight.
Stereo reverbs: wide spread is good for blend; narrow it when treating mono sounds so the effect is not exposed, or when drum spots pair with narrow room mics.
Never judge reverb/effects by on-off alone (loudness bias); drop the dry+wet pair out for a few seconds then reintroduce.
Pad rule: if you can hear the pad it is too loud.
Boost then cut trick: set pad/reverb a bit loud, then EQ it back to taste.
More blend reverb pushes a sound back; dry instrument stays upfront.
Check balances at different volumes and on different monitors after adding reverb.
Some elements deliberately poorly blended (dry) stay right in your face.
Rough mixes: referencing them avoids missing parts; do not stray far if client lived with it long.
After widening, recheck balance of center instruments.
Switch between mix and reference instantly; match subjective loudness (not meter peaks).
LUFS Integrated (EBU R128) meter can match levels objectively.
Compare a loudness-processed version of your mix when referencing against mastered releases.
Check mono for reverbs, wideners, and delays; cheap reverbs fail in mono.
Use multiple monitoring systems and low/high listening levels; headphones magnify distortion artifacts.
Reverb amount and low cut are genre specific; check against commercial references.
Do ABX/blind toggles to fight confirmation bias.
Masking meters: only act on problems heard; some masking is wanted for blend.
Evaluating a processor only by on/off (louder sounds better).
Exciter/high-frequency enhancement fatigues ears, gets overdone.
De-essing too hard causes lisp.
Sub-synth out of phase with bass fundamental makes bass thinner.
Boosting more than needed or many narrow boosts.
Multiband on every band, using defaults/presets or auto gain compensation.
Using reverb reflexively.
Long reverb on pads blurs chord changes; long low-end reverb robs headroom.
Heavy master compression until side effects (lost transients, pumping, low-end weight loss) dominate.
Wide Haas delay on key parts blurs detail.
Ducking/masking removal everywhere: hollow, unblended mix.
Multiband buss compressor hides balance problems and encourages overprocessing.
Putting mono delay returns globally: narrows mix.
Distortion adds harmonics related to the source; use as send for control; drive amount matters most. Parallel distortion needs phase checks.
Low-end layering: sub sine, triangle for blend, mono; simple parallel MIDI sub follow-up.
Pitch-shift layer for density: octave up easiest, mix low.
Double bass with sub-synth following the bass notes for solid low end.

Reverb enhancements: blend, size, tone, sustain, spread. Blend: short natural preset, 10-20 ms pre-delay. Size: tail-focused, pre-delay 50 ms or more. Sustain: pre-delay at least 25 ms. Tone: sub-10 ms pre-delay for strongest comb filtering.
Blend reverb with first ~0.5 s responsible for blending.
Delay: blend slapback 50 to 100 ms with little feedback; ms = 60000/BPM (120 bpm = 500 ms, also 250, 125, triplets about 167 and 83).
Tempo-synced delays sit in mix; unsynced pop out; polyrhythmic (3/8, 3/16) for dance.
Subtle eighth-note delay on drums buss adds rhythmic energy; overdoing drags.
Bypass rule: sudden pre-delay larger than ~20 ms in short reverbs can cause flams.
Gated "fake" reverb: dense burst of echoes, threshold-independent.
Add atmosphere layers (room tone, hiss, vinyl, film sounds) to blend and add depth in electronic/overdubbed productions.
Room tone/noise improves blend.
Pre-delay reduces wet masking by dry.
Quick spectrum: boost-high-frequency compress for brightness (spectral dynamics).
Linear-phase EQ useful for parallel returns.
Reference a finished first mix section against commercial tracks before building the rest.
Save a new project version before any further changes, so you can go back.
Build the arrangement by muting active tracks, looping one section, then bringing tracks back in rank order of importance.
Use multing when several changes apply to one track at once; use automation when only a couple of parameters change.
Automation is treated as close to a prerequisite for competitive pop-style mixes.
Leave detailed rides until multing and dynamics processing have failed. Rides are labor-heavy and hard to edit later.
Do a top-to-tail listen, then a snag list the next morning, then re-reference on all monitors.
Check master-buss processing once all tracks and effects of the first section are running, then adjust balance.
Assignment order: master-buss, reference, balance the rest by importance, full draft, reference again, snag list, client feedback, then alternate versions and stems.
Overall tonality check: if references have less 300-500Hz energy than your mix, try EQ in that zone (master buss or channels).
Do not force a spectral match onto a reference curve. Different mixes should differ.
Piano and acoustic guitar often need strong low cuts in a busy mix. The same cut thins them out when they become the featured part. Reassess the low cut when the part moves forward.
Metal kick and bass clash: an EQ on the kick rolled up to about 44Hz, automated, keeps low kick energy from masking bass. Some mixes need both a level change and this EQ.
Dip a snare-hit frequency around 1kHz or 700Hz per hit, timed to the transient, to keep the decay fuller. This is an extreme rock-production example.
Nasal or dull consonants (n, ng, m, l) benefit from emphasis. Emphasis around vowel transitions can imply level.
Audible range assumed: 20Hz to 20kHz.
Pitch of a note is set by its fundamental. Harmonics at whole-number multiples set timbre. Darker sounds are richer in lows; brighter sounds are stronger in highs.
A +6dB level change doubles voltage (100mV to 200mV).
Multiband compression: gain reduction in each band depends on that band's level, so changes in instrumentation can shift overall tone.
Multiband distortion or saturation can raise perceived loudness with little peak increase. Side effects: harshness, sibilance, veiled midrange.
Clipping, flat-topped or soft-rounded, appears in many chart tracks. It keeps drum attacks more intact than peak limiting. Side effects: tonal change, distortion on steady sounds.
A chart track shown had clusters of 70 to 150 clipped samples.
Loudness lift needs several processes; if the target is not reached without damage, change the mix.
Client-facing loud bounces are common. Keep an unprocessed mixdown archive so loudness can be redone later.
Rides on a single cymbal crash can be about 5dB or more.
Note-tail or quiet detail rides can be 6dB or more. A small balance change can be a quarter of a dB.
Near the bottom of a fader, steps can be 1dB or more. Keep faders in their best-resolution area.
A fader lift of about 10dB at a line end can reveal quiet vocal detail.
Syllable-by-syllable rides in fast rap-style delivery use a short gain pulse at weak syllables.
Bad compression can be partly fixed by compressing more, then rebuilding dynamics with faders. Expect lots of automation on vocals.
Compress first, use automated de-essing or a keyed ducker on reverb before using many manual rides.
Dropping a pop vocal to a set level per syllable can take about two hours on a four-minute song.
Keyed multiband thresholds can move per word on vocals.
Build-ups: depend less on level increases, because loudness processing reduces them. Use arrangement density, timbre, reverb or width instead.
Keep the peak of a build-up fixed to the production's long-term peak. Drop the energy before the build.
Widen chorus only if it fits. Wider acoustic guitars, opposed-panned doubles, or Haas delays make the chorus feel bigger.
Super-dry choruses: the hook jumps forward in depth against wetter verses.
Opposite approach: keep room mics in verses and remove them in choruses so the guitar gets the space. (record both sides with the above)
Verses: drier and closer; choruses: wetter and bigger. Reverb and delay levels can ride over the track.
Cut reverb or delay tails right before a verse to make the verse hit.
Opening up bandwidth in a chorus (filters in verses, full range in chorus) adds weight.
Stereo ideas: keep the image consistent across regions of the spectrum. Check width separately in low, mid, high bands.
Pad levels need automation over sections so they support without standing out. EQ may also be needed where they are masked.
Master-buss width moves can change the response of instruments further down the chain. Recheck.
Balance check order: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal first. These leave the least room within a genre.
Compare each instrument's dynamic range against references, not just its level.
Fine balance rides: listen at low volume. Loud listening turns small moves into a blur.
Keep monitor level constant during balance rides. Think in distance, not just level.
Keep a bass note from out-booming others. Automate the note or dig in with EQ.
Lift a background detail for a moment, then return. A short imbalance often goes unnoticed.
When lifting one part, dip competing background parts to reduce masking.
Lead vocal: aim for intelligibility first, then emotion through fader rides on breath, starts, and tails.
Vocal-first logic: check that someone unfamiliar can hear every word.
Use faders instead of EQ or compression for vocals in some styles.
Fader moves matter more than EQ on some chart productions. The arrangement must build.
Overall loudness: pick a level and stay near it for judgments. Use the same monitor level throughout.
Reference against commercial tracks at loudness-matched levels. Add a loudness processor only for comparison, then judge the sound with the boost removed.
Reference against the client's rough mix, which may be louder.
Loudness-normalised streaming now shapes what loudness means; test how the mix sounds in that context.
Test-master: loudness-match the master to your unmastered mix. Judge for distortion, low-end loss, drum ducking.
Use a small reference speaker that approximates consumer playback, and check the full mix on several systems.
Snag on consumer systems (car, earbuds, hi-fi) after the monitoring checks, not before.
Hide DAW meters and the playhead when judging a snag. Visual cues bias perception.
Snags: write them down, check across all monitors, keep only those that hold on every system.
Listening rule: if a problem bothers you on three full plays in a row, fix it.
Morning ears are fresher; schedule final snags then.
Expecting mastering to fix a mix. Dissatisfaction with the mix is a mix problem.
Matching EQ curves exactly to a reference.
Endless revisions and recalls. A mix rarely improves after many rounds.
Riding too early. Rides before balance is settled waste time.
Fiddling with mix settings to fit one monitor.
Judging loudness-processed mixes without removing the boost.
Using heavy levels or reverb to force excitement. Loudness processing flattens it.
Over-reliance on a single de-esser or dynamics tool instead of musical rides.
Save a version before major automation, and archive the unprocessed mix.
Keep backups in two places, and keep every client revision version.
Album: duplicate one or two key chains for family sound, rebuild the rest.
Album: use a separate project with all bounced mixes to check balance and tone across songs.
Mastering should not be the first answer to a weak mix. Use it for album consistency and format delivery.
Mastering engineer: test-master one track before committing; expect candid communication.
Hardware faders: good for many automation points; the mouse is enough for a few critical points.
Reverb or delay tails can be pushed up for interest when nothing else is happening.
Sound speed used in the book: about 343 m/s.
Sample rate and bit depth set analog-to-digital fidelity.
Mastering = editing, cleanup, leveling, processing, output to final medium; sequencing and spacing are part of the job.
Gain: raise the whole album's level by the same amount if group-adjusting; never fix song levels per song by peak.

Do leveling before limiting. After a limiter, levels can only go down; EQ or filtering after limiting undoes peak protection and can create new intersample overs. To change levels between tunes, go back to the unlimited source.
Big level moves belong in the highest-precision processor, not in a low-resolution DAW; fewer calculations in the chain is better.
Sample rate conversion is next-to-last step; dither to the shortest wordlength is last.
Processing at a higher sample rate sounds better, then downsample and dither at the end.
Leave final loudness tools to the mastering stage; mixers should not pre-limit hard.
A mastering pass can improve a mix by roughly one letter grade; some problems are better fixed in the mix, so send a preliminary mix early and remix if severe.
Mastering from stems lets you rebalance leads vs rhythm after processing.
Always compare final master against the unprocessed source; if the source sounds better, rework.
If any tic or noise is found in QC, redo and relisten to the entire master; headphones reveal more noises than speakers.
Log all settings, gains, and revisions so changes can be reproduced; keep a high-resolution capture in case old settings cannot be recalled.
Peak meter level says almost nothing about loudness; the ear follows average level. Two takes peaking at -4 dB and 0 dB can be equally loud; raising the -4 dB one by 4 dB makes it 4 dB louder.
Typical mixdown peak-to-average: 14 to 18 dB (rarely 20); raw unprocessed digital tracks 18-20 dB above 0 VU; analog tape peaks up to 14 dB above 0 VU.
Peak-to-average (crest) lost by tape saturation partly comes from added harmonics; a harmonic generator also lowers crest.
Loudness war: hot recordings do not play louder on radio; radio limiters just cut back and dull them. Heavy clipping gives fatigue and short listening time.
Dynamic, high-transient masters sound "compressed" on small systems, which compress by themselves; reducing transients in mastering makes small systems worse, not better.
Over-compression is hard to judge on compressing monitors (near-fields, small tube amps), so use wide-range, high-power monitors.
Class difference by genre: a string quartet and a pop-teen act need different approaches; same tool settings should not be reused across styles.
Modern CDs can pin a VU meter whatever the calibration; a K-System style meter is the proposed fix.
Music with a ballad that is compressed can end up louder than a rock track under peak normalization; match by ear/average.
Warmer: boost about 200-600 Hz or dip about 3-7 kHz; these are a yin-yang pair.
Edgy/harsh: excess energy about 4-7 kHz (tough on high brass); cutting 2.5-8 kHz often sweetens it.
Boxy: excess about 300-800 Hz; the next third-octave up reads as nasal.
Thin: deficiency from about 75 to 600 Hz.
Male vocal power sits near 250 Hz; adding highs can mask or depress the lower mids, so the vocal loses power on limited-bandwidth systems.
Midrange is the key to translation: a good recording still works filtered below 200 Hz and above 5 kHz.
Boosts are heard more readily than dips; use dips where needed.
Adding highs to compensate for dull monitors is a mistake: it becomes harsh on good systems and radio limiters cut it back.
A hat brim or similar obstacle notches roughly 2 kHz (ear example of coloration).
Presence is an upper-mid strength; too much is fatiguing.
Comb filtering is very hard to fix with EQ and EQ in mastering affects the whole mix; fix upstream. Delays near 1 ms per foot; if one mic is 10 dB lower, comb effects become insignificant.
Pop vocals commonly have extra lower-mid and presence from proximity effect; aim for enough to sound larger-than-life without mud, sibilance, or edge.
Brightness trade-off: mastering that is skewed bright fails on small treble-heavy systems; skewed dull or bassy fails on bass-heavy ones. Aim at the middle of the bell curve.
Lowered air absorption means a gentle high-frequency rolloff usually sounds right, amount varying with room size and speaker distance.
Check mono/fold-down compatibility (stereo to mono) when finalizing.
Left and right dither/random numbers must be different or stereo separation is compromised.
Near-field mixes often show: boomy kick (esp. NS-10 style), low vocal, low reverb, depressed bass midrange (about low-mid comb/resonance), narrow stereo separation.

Bass: accurate subwoofers are essential; without them you miss vocal pops, rumble, mic vibration, and lowest notes. Too-hot subs lead to masters that do not translate. Extra important for hip-hop and reggae.
Extreme bass-heavy club/car/boombox systems: do not master to them; make a separate dedicated master for those venues.
Client asking for very hot bass: demonstrate on a boomy alternate system; boosting for that sound overdrives typical car systems and sounds wrong elsewhere.
Bass imbalance (a muddy, uneven, too-loud bass from small-speaker mixing) was fixed with EQ plus dual-band upward expansion.
One pair of accurate, wide-range, high-headroom speakers; no little alternate speakers in the room; alternates elsewhere as double-check only.
Louder monitoring makes a mix feel bassier; a mix made too loud sounds bass-shy when played quietly (equal-loudness effect). Do not master at excessive level.
Judge monitors against 25 to 50 reference recordings and average; re-check after changing amps, cables, converters.
Use one fixed D/A and a fixed monitor gain to compare your master against commercial CDs.
Ear training: recognize 1/3-octave ranges with pink noise; test bandwidth limiting (5 kHz bandwidth removes life and clarity); learn overload sounds; know what great purist recordings sound like.
Compare master with accurate refs on several systems; notes that cancel out suggest balance is right.
Test low-level behavior: attenuate music by about 40 dB and listen with headphones for ambience and noise character.
Treat every album as a concept album; song order, spacing, and levels shape emotional response.
Never auto-normalize individual songs; level by ear (average loudness), not peak.
Gap spacing example from a log: extra 1/2 second added between tunes after review; spacing is set by feel and checked in context.
Non-linear workflow: revisit earlier songs after setting a climax track; easy ending-big then beginning-soft transitions need gain/EQ care.
Albums made by band members risk "more me" balance; avoid with a neutral producer.
Sequencing advice starts with not responding purely to intellectual or theme ordering.
Bit math: about 6 dB per bit; 16-bit about 96 dB range, 24-bit about 144 dB.
16-bit dither (TPDF) sits about -91 dBFS RMS; the noise floor rises about 4.77 dB. Perceived dynamic range can reach about 115 dB with dither though measured SNR is about 91 dB.
Always dither when reducing wordlength; dither once, as the final step only; avoid cumulative 16-bit dithering and 16-bit intermediate storage.
Truncation to 24 bits is far less bothersome than truncation to 16.

Dither alone on a 16-bit source without gain raises the noise about 3 dB; raising a 16-bit source 10 dB then redithering worsens SNR about 2.4 dB. Small gain changes on 16-bit sources are not worth it.

Noise-shaped dither moves noise away from about 3 kHz sensitivity toward 10-22 kHz; best versions are tonally neutral and give about 19-20 bit feel on 16-bit CD. Flat dither may suit some rock; pristine acoustic material sounds veiled when over-dithered.
Dither flavors sound different; audition per genre; the most transparent may not suit "grungy" rock.
Any gain change or EQ increases wordlength; process at 24-bit or longer and keep outputs at 24-bit. 16-bit sources can be bounced to 24-bit for processing.
Auto-dither: turn dither off when the source is already at the destination wordlength, to avoid dithering twice.
Peak OVER definition: 3 contiguous full-scale samples (about 33 microseconds at 44.1 kHz); more samples may be allowed at higher rates.

Digital OVER meters can miss intersample peaks; true intersample peaks may reach about 3 dB above 0 dBFS (text says up to 13 dB in the OCR; likely 3), so stay below about -3 dBFS on non-oversampling meters, or use a limiter ceiling of about -0.2 dB with an oversampling limiter/meter.
Filters and EQ, even attenuating ones, can cause overs; sample-rate converters and codecs (MP3/AC3) can also overload near full scale; keep peaks at or below about -0.2 dBFS for post-processing.
Turning level down after clipping does not remove the distortion, only hides it from the meter; some consumer D/As stay distorted 200-700 ms after intersample overs.
For 24-bit recording, peaking at -3 to -10 dBFS costs nothing in SNR; a 16-bit recording fits in the bottom 96 dB of a 24-bit file (48 dB lost to reach 16-bit SNR).
Hot mixes force an extra attenuation stage before mastering EQ/SRC; mixes peaking -3 dBFS or lower are easier to process.
Calibration references: -20 dBFS = 0 VU (US/broadcast, suggested), -18 dBFS (European), -14 dBFS (analog tape). Analog PPMs are slower (6-10 ms); allow about 5 dB lead.
Analog gain staging: amplifiers should clip at least 6 dB above music peaks; with 0 VU = +4 dBu, clip point around +30 dBu minimum; keep about 26 dB between nominal level and clip.
Digital chains: about 24 dB internal headroom above 0 dBFS is enough; 24-bit chain noise about -139 dBFS.
Normalization never improves SNR or sound quality; it only adds a calculation.
CD error rules of thumb: BLER under 100 and no E32 errors; Exabyte error percentage under 0.1% (0.2-0.3% tolerable without retries).
Delivery media for CD plants: DDP (best, most popular), PCM-1630, CDR; CDR least reliable. Send DDP with PQ at head unless the plant agrees otherwise.
Written PQ list is still required by plants; ISRC and emphasis flags are recorded.
Audio loadback/null test only proves no uncorrectable errors, not media health.
Normalizing each song individually.
Mixing on colored mini-monitors and trusting them; boosting highs to fix dull speakers.
Clipping then lowering level to "hide" overs.
Truncating to 16 bits without dither; multiple generations of 16-bit dither.
Trusting a digital processor's bypass; test for bit transparency.
Setting subs hot to impress clients.
Applying heavy compression "for small speakers."
Mixing from analog PPM/VU peaks without allowing for slow attack.
Treating gear lists or "magic" settings as the answer; each tool gives incremental gain.
Using an extreme car/club system as the common reference.
A tool can't replace ears; a clean preferred reference is the engineer's own monitor, not a measurement.
Musical language: 262 Hz about middle C, 440 Hz A; octave is 2x or half; 225 Hz near low English horn/viola.
Mastering for the middle of the bell curve satisfies the most listeners; peaks are easier to hear than dips.
Documentation/backups: keep logs plus an in-house backup after approval; archive formats age.
Section 1 end: Chapter 7 begins on sequencing; text cut at ma-056 mid-chapter.
Sequence the album before leveling and processing; later songs depend on the order.
Build a rough playlist, note each song's mood in a word or two, and grade the strongest songs.
Group songs into sets of about 1 to 4 songs, with a larger gap between sets than inside them.
Test each song-to-song join by playing the last 30 to 40 s of one song into the start of the next.
Fix a key clash by adding spacing or swapping in a song with a similar feel and compatible key.
Process the loudest song first, save its settings, then work through the album in order.
Check edits and joins last: review tracks 1 and 2 again after the final song is done.
Judge processing with the monitor gain held constant so each song is compared fairly.
Mix engineers should send unfaded, uncut material so mastering can shape fades and tops.
Keep a safe version (unprocessed or digital) alongside any version with analog-style tail problems.
Pop dynamic range is typically 6 to 10 dB; some forms have 1 dB, and 15 dB is very rare.
Soft passages 8 to 15 dB below peak feel effective only briefly in pop; acoustic forms can keep them for minutes.
Judge level by ear in context, not by meter readings; a meter misreads soft passages after loud ones.
Raise a too-soft intro with fader moves of about 1/4 to 1/2 dB, or with a fast edit at the intro-to-body join.
Make big changes in the soft passage just before a crescendo; the 1 to 1.5 dB drop example is a crossfade of about 12 s.
Lower a previous song by a few tenths of a dB rather than squashing the loudest song.
Compressor ratios used in music mastering are mostly about 1.5:1 to 3:1; some use 5:1.
Typical compressor thresholds sit around -20 to -10 dBFS, placed where the musical accents are.
For nearly invisible control, try a 1.01 to 1.1 ratio with a threshold near -30 to -40 dBFS.
Compressor attack typically 50 to 300 ms (average about 100 ms); release 50 to 500 ms (average 150 to 250 ms).
Start a mastering release around 250 ms and tune from there.
Attack and release both under about 50 ms cause waveform-following distortion.
Compressors with a crest-factor control range from RMS to peak; RMS-sensing sounds more natural per the author.
Limiting alone can raise loudness with little harm; compression changes the inner dynamics more.
An 18 to 20 dB true peak-to-average source can often go to about 14 dB with little clarity loss.
Short transients (a few ms) of unprocessed digital material can be reduced by about 4 to 6 dB.
Analog-tape sources have already lost short transients, so further transient reduction is more audible.
Manual gain drops of 1 to 3 dB lasting under about 3 ms can be nearly invisible.
Auto-release limiters range about 50 to 150 ms; a very short release only fits very short peaks.
Parallel (upward) compression: threshold around -50 dBFS, attack 1 ms or less, ratio 2:1 to 2.5:1.
Parallel compression release: 250 to 350 ms, up to about 500 ms for a cappella reverb.
Parallel compression output: about -5 to -15 dB makeup for subtle use.
Parallel compression dry path needs a matched delay, typically 5 to 10 samples, found by nulling polarity.
Upward expansion ratios are very mild: about 1:1.01 to 1:1.2 (decimal 0.99 to 0.83).
Upward expansion attacks run about 1 ms to 300 ms; above about 150 ms, reconsider the process.
Expanders need output attenuation because makeup gain can overload the output.
Macro-dynamics (section-to-section loudness) suit manual gain riding; micro-dynamics (hits, syllables) suit processors.
Downward compression tends to lower the song's macro range, and loud sections lose impact.
Monitor gain: higher monitoring makes over-compression less likely.
VU reading: about 0 VU equals -20 dBFS peak on a sine, or up to about -14 dBFS; reading hot can mean over-compression.
Multiband compression: one or two bands are usually enough; more than two is rare.
Split bands to keep a heavy bass drum from modulating the rest of the mix.
For sibilance, compress only roughly 2.5 to 9 kHz (3 to 9 kHz in one example).
Bus compression at about 1 dB, with slow attack and release, is a gentle mix-stage option.
The symphony balance (gradual high rolloff) is a good general reference, though rolloff varies by style.
Build the midrange first; the vocal, guitar, and piano fundamentals must be right before anything else.
Use a spectrum analyzer for discrete noise and extreme lows and highs, not for musical balance.
Reggae often wants more bass; punk often sounds thin and bright on purpose.
Parametric EQ has center frequency, bandwidth (Q), and gain.
Q equals center frequency divided by 3 dB bandwidth. Example: -17 dB at 50 Hz with Q 4 is 0.36 octave.
Example: +17 dB at 2 kHz with Q 0.86 is 1.6 octave wide.
Gentle Q values of 0.6 to 0.7 sound more natural; Q above 2 is for surgical work.
Find a resonance: large boost, wide Q, sweep, narrow Q, then cut.
Gerzon resonant shelf example: Q 0.71 bass shelf near 178 Hz with a dip just above it.
Air band is about 15 to 20 kHz; avoid air boosts that make cymbals jump forward or sound harsh.
Baxandall high boost: parametric at about 20 kHz, Q about 1, gives a slow rise from about 10 kHz.
A 3 dB/octave shelf approximates the Baxandall slope.
High-pass example at 61 Hz is sharp; low-pass example at 3364 Hz is gentle; both at -3 dB points.
Hiss is most audible near 3 kHz; a 1 to 4 dB dip at 3 to 5 kHz is a more surgical fix than a low-pass filter.
Yin and yang: a dip near 250 Hz can act like a boost near 5 kHz; bass makes highs seem duller.
Harsh trumpets: dip around 6 to 8 kHz and/or boost near 250 Hz.
Lost air from a 1/2 dB cut near 7 kHz can often be restored with about 1/4 dB at 15 to 20 kHz.
Changes under about 1/2 dB are audible with good monitoring; still, do not judge EQ by instant A/B.
Play each EQ setting for at least about 30 s, sometimes minutes, before switching.
Bass fundamental often sits around 62 to 125 Hz, with harmonics from 125 to 250 Hz and up.
Some crash cymbals have fundamentals as low as about 1.5 kHz.
Bass drum fundamentals can sit under 60 Hz, but bass drum harmonics often overlap the bass guitar.
Low bass energy below 50 Hz needs about 6 to 10 dB more power for equal loudness; 50 to 100 Hz needs about 3 to 5 dB more.
Consider a sharp high-pass below about 40 Hz to save bass energy, but only with a monitor that is calibrated at low end.
A steep 80 Hz filter is fine on an isolated vocal; rare on a full mix.
Narrow the bass boost around 80 Hz if it muddies the vocal.
Boosting the highs can thin the lower midrange and make cymbals louder too.
Check monitor balance first with mono pink noise centered between speakers.
Stereo balance errors above 0.2 dB are significant; aim for under 0.1 dB.
Meters are poor judges of channel balance; a mandolin on one side can read higher and still be correct.
Reversed relative polarity causes hollow sound, wide imaging, and lost bass.
Find relative polarity by switching to mono and flipping one channel; the version with more bass is correct.
Fix small inter-channel timing with a sample-based delay, aiming for maximum highs and least comb filter in mono.
DC offset: a steep high-pass below about 20 Hz is the simplest fix; check by starting and stopping playback.
Mid/side encode: M = 0.5*(L+R), S = 0.5*(L-R); decode L = M+S, R = M-S (check level by 6 dB).
With more M, the sound is more centered; with more S, it spreads wider.
Mute M and you hear a hole in the middle; mute S and the vocal sounds alone and narrow.
Raise a centered vocal by adding a channel-reversed copy at about -12 to -16 dB (too much makes it mono).
Use EQ on the M channel only, for example 250 Hz and 5 kHz, to lift a centered vocal.
Compress only M to bring up the center when it gets loud, or compress M and expand S.
Use a mid/side fix for boomy bass only when a remix is not possible; it keeps the vocal balanced.
Stems must be sample-accurate and start at the same timestamp, or they can cancel.
Bass drum leakage into vocal and piano mics can be heard on a subwoofer; fix it in mixing with selective high-pass.
A calibrated monitor has repeatable gain marked in decibels.
Compare processed and unprocessed at matched loudness; louder sounds better in an instant A/B.
Use a monitor that squashes the sound only as a warning: a squashed reference can hide needed compression.
Small-system listening: a master that sticks out a little on a high-headroom system may be fine on small systems.
Poor monitors hide over-compression; a high-headroom room reveals it.
Use a noisy listening room or fan noise to test whether soft passages are too soft.
A tube amp self-compresses and can hide mix problems that show up in mastering.
Calibrated monitor gain makes mixes consistent across rooms.
Opening track must be favorable and usually up-tempo; the first song sets the album tone.
A set can open with a ballad and end with a driving song, depending on the end mood of the prior set.
Odd-one-out songs can work as a one-song set in the middle, with clear pauses before and after.
Pacing: fast-to-fast is short, fast-to-slow is medium, slow-to-fast is long.
Never count seconds between songs; judge the gap by feel.
Very short gaps after fade-outs are usually right, because listeners in cars do not hear the tail.
Vinyl noise fills LP gaps; an LP-to-CD master often needs 2 or more seconds removed.
Mystery spaces: try long and short gaps and move them until one is obvious.
Ending: follow the climax with one or two easy songs, not a big uptempo encore.
Do not judge a space by only the tail and head; judge over the whole set in context.
A tight start followed by normal gaps makes normal gaps feel too long.
Redbook CD: no official pause shorter than 2 s; shorter gaps are fine but have no index-0 pause.
Track start: fastest players cue in 1 SMPTE frame, slowest about 5 frames; place marks to avoid pre-noise.
Put applause or intros in the index-0 gap so random play skips them; the gap does not count toward track length.
Some players and software ignore index 0; treat that as a limit on what the gap can do.
Check CD-R copies: some duplicators mute the gap, even replacing much of it with 2 s of silence.
Minimum CD track length is 4 s. Up to 99 tracks; up to 99 indexes per track.
Use disc-at-once writing; track-at-once and standalone recorders can add errors and lack index 0.
Sample-based offsets: a 12-frame offset is about 160 ms; check PQ display with and without it.
Processor latency can reach about 12 SMPTE frames; measure it and move PQ marks by that amount.
Hidden pregap tracks are not Redbook; only CD-R masters can carry them.
75 CD frames per second, versus 30 SMPTE frames per second.
Internal DSP at 48-bit fixed point, dithered to 24 bits on output, is a good-quality chain for digital output.
Avoid hard clipping; it produces square-wave distortion. Prefer a good limiter.
Oversampled clipping reduces artifacts, but the author is not convinced it is a fix.
Sample rate: the book's 44.1 kHz appears as "4.4.1 kHz" in this OCR text.
Use a sample rate converter with clean conversion, but prefer SRC over pitch-and-time correctors.
Consider the reverb tail on a fade when a fade-out must be extended; send both edited and unedited.
Chasing loudness until it is squashed; a louder master can sound worse.
Mixing through a compressor on the mix bus; a bus processor may ruin the mix.
Starting every limiter at a fixed threshold preset (about -6 dBFS) is not a judgment; adjust by ear.
Trusting a single instant A/B to decide EQ.
Applying a long fade that cuts off reverb tails; use a shorter or S-shaped fade.
Editing a retake that cuts off reverb; have the performer start earlier for a running start.
Trusting the meter: it misses that a too-soft intro needs raising.
Adding bass to fix a mix: it raises bass relative to the vocal.
Expecting multiband compression to fix a bad mix; it causes odd tonality if overused.
Mixing aggressive bus compression that cannot be undone.
Compressing before EQ when the EQ boost is meant to add level; the compressor can undo it.
Parallel compression: keep the dry path matched to the compressor delay so no comb filtering occurs.
A signal 20 dB or more below the main path barely changes the total level.
Noise reduction: a narrow expander can remove 1 to 4 dB in the 3 to 5 kHz range with ratios under 1:2 (e.g. 1:1.1).
Remove hiss only where it is distracting; the ear masks noise under music.
P-pops: a brief high-pass around 100 Hz (sometimes up to 400 Hz) can remove them invisibly.
Hum and buzz: roughly 25 narrow notch filters at Q 40 or higher can clear a hum preset.
Noise sampling: a sample of about 1 s of noise without signal is enough for noise-removal tools.
Keep a pre-downbeat piece of an intro untouched so noise samples and edits are clean.
Dynamic EQ acts like a rumble filter or noise gate at low levels; a delicate classical piece may suit it.
Mix engineers should avoid exciters on the mix bus; mastering is the place for exciting.
Exciters and MaxxBass-style tools can make mixes thin if overused.
Each manual de-click, de-thump, or de-pop should be checked against the source before accepting.
A simple multi-band rule of thumb: two bands is safer than more because multiband adds phase shift.
Mix with conservative average levels; quality lost in mixing cannot be restored later
Mix pop to a fixed monitor position and keep transients clean; mastering then has room to add loudness
Keep the monitor fixed; if a master gets too loud, reduce the processing rather than the monitor
Some recordings are best left alone; processing gains can be less than processing losses
Source-quality rule: start at the highest resolution and keep it as long as possible
Sample-rate conversion goes second-to-last, then dither as the final step
Cut the number of generations; go back a generation when a new process is needed
Do analog processing before the single A/D conversion when possible
Remaster from unprocessed sources where they exist; undo loudness-race damage
Calibrated monitor: 0 dB position = 83 dB SPL with pink noise
Calibration pink noise is -20 dBFS RMS; peaks sit near 0 dBFS
Crest factor = peak minus average level; example: -20 dBFS average, -3 dBFS peak = 17 dB
Typical mixed material: crest 10 to 18 dB; calibrated mixes may peak -10 to -2 dBFS
Extreme normal-music crest about 20 dB; a 20 dB crest at -20 dBFS average never overloads
Average vs peak: average means RMS; a simple mean can err by about 2 dB
Peaks in a good recording can be about 20 dB above average
Higher monitor position tends to mean higher crest factor; lower position means compressed average
Classical and acoustic jazz with no compression: 0 dB monitor position
Pop: -6 dB is the lowest monitor position that still sounds good; crest about 14 dB
Pop made before about 1993 sounds right at -6 dB
Skilled masters can work at -7 or -8 dB, but quality drops
Some hypercompressed pop CDs run about 6 dB hotter than the -6 dB reference
Mixing pop: keep the monitor between 0 and -6 dB
Room size: a large room needs about 2 dB more gain; a small remote truck about 2 dB less
Loudness race: digital limiting let average level sit near peak level, about 20 dB above old averages
Hot pop CDs can differ by about 15 dB in average level; some by 8 to 12 dB
K-System: K-20, K-14, K-12 meters; 0 dB = 83 dBC, and the monitor gain is tied to the meter
K-20 for wide-range material (classical, film, audiophile); K-14 for moderately compressed pop, rock, folk
K-12 is for broadcast material only
Typical monitor positions in a medium room: K-20 0 dB, K-14 -6 dB, K-12 -8 dB
K-14 needs 6 dB less monitor gain than K-20 for the same loudness
Fortissimo (red) zone: +3 to +4 on the average scale for loud large-ensemble passages
Rock and pop can use the red zone for climaxes, but only occasionally
Constant use of the red zone suggests a monitor problem or overcompression
Film mixes: 83 dB SPL reference with about 20 dB headroom above it
Pop studio: about 14 dB headroom above 83 dB
Pop at -6 dB monitor gives about 77 dB SPL with -20 dBFS pink noise
Dorrough meter: the AVG zero point sits 14 dB below full scale
VU meter: its 300 ms integration does not match real loudness; top half of scale covers only 6 dB
Cassette: average no higher than +3 over 185 nW/m; high-frequency peaks above about +5 to +6 distort
Classical with low crest: avoid peaking to full scale; keep monitor at 0 dB and use K-20
Pop with crest well under 14 dB should not be peaked to full scale
Legacy overcompressed CDs: reduce gain on remaster so average falls within K-14
Avoid monitor EQ; fix room problems acoustically first
Bass should not sound lumpy; subs should only add weight to the lowest notes
Sub crossover: choose the low-pass that splices most smoothly, often about 40 to 80 Hz (OCR reads 4.0; likely 40)
Sub target: extend the satellites down to about 25 Hz
Crossover at 60 Hz or below: sub is hard to notice except for solidity
LFE check: the 50 or 63 Hz band reads 10 dB above the 1 kHz band (78 dB SPL)
Dolby Digital check: test with a mono crossover at 100 Hz
Typical bass management: 4th-order (24 dB/oct) low-pass on woofer, 2nd-order (12 dB/oct) high-pass on satellites
Treble rolloff with distance: lower high end pushes a sound back in depth
Steep low-pass filters add pre-echo; pre-echo length = inverse of transition bandwidth (500 Hz gives 2 ms)
Gentle low-pass filtering may be the better trade-off; a 50 kHz gentle-filter sample rate is the stated minimum
Phantom center: L/R must match within +/- 0.1 dB at 1 kHz
Five uncorrelated channels sum about 7 dB above one channel (+/- 1 dB) in the midband
Theatre surrounds sit 3 dB below fronts; home music sets all five equal
Sub gain: set the sub level with the RTA; spread subs if mono bass rises by 1 dB
Subs near walls raise deep bass; move them to flatten the response
Center bass: high-pass the center to match the L/R speakers, then trim the bass level
Surround bass: favor the mono pink-noise result, since bass usually stays in phase
Correlation meter: readings near center mean less channel correlation and a wider image; check mono fold-down
Haas delay fuses correlated sounds; uncorrelated reverb spreads to surrounds
Haas fusion window: echoes within about 40 ms fuse with the direct sound
Haas delays of 12 to 40 ms can add clarity; 1 foot = 1 ms
Short delays under about 5 ms blur the center image; mono image wobbles with timing errors
Spaced omnis: a third center omni stabilizes center image
Comb filtering: mic spacing should be 3 times mic-to-source distance (3:1 rule)
A single delay on a spot mic cannot replace room reflections; adjust in 1 ms steps
Speakers: flat response, good to about 60 Hz; each capable of 103 dB SPL before clipping
Monitor matrix: flexible bass management with repeatable calibrated gains
Measurement: calibrated 1/3-octave RTA with spatial averaging; a sound level meter is less accurate
Rope method: loudspeakers on a circle; front L/R at +/- 30 degrees, surrounds at +/- 110 degrees (ITU accepts 100 to 120)
Sub polarity normal, phase 0 degrees to start; delay 1 ms = 1 foot
RTA averaging of 3 to 10 s; wait before reading
Smooth response within +/- 3 dB; fix anomalies acoustically first
Wideband SPL meter (C weighting, slow) is a fallback with 2 to 3 dB error
If the monitor control drifts down over time, quality is probably falling
Judge the sub by listening with it on and off; it should add weight, not be heard
Equal-loudness: mix at a fixed level, or the mix may sound bass-shy at lower levels
Near-field monitors on console meter bridges kill most sense of depth
Correlation meter beats an oscilloscope for stereo checks; always confirm with ears
Keep the monitor fixed across an album so loudness matches track to track
Mark boxes or files with the K-meter and calibration used (e.g. K-14/RMS)
Stereo CD and 5.1 DVD should match loudness; a 6 dB difference is the limit the book sets
A K-20 CD will not jump in loudness against a K-20 DVD in the same player
Consumers adjust volume per record, so the loudness race has no fixed reference
16-bit properly dithered: theoretical noise floor about -91.2 dBFS RMS
Processing needs more headroom; purist work may need 48 to 72 bits
POW-R type 3 dither reaches 20-bit-like performance near 3.5 kHz
Single-precision 24-bit truncation: even a 10 dB boost adds distortion; 40-bit float or higher is cleaner
Double sampling reduces aliasing in compressors and limiters
Undithered truncation sounds gritty; dither keeps noise benign
Bitscope: 16 active bits on a dithered signal is normal; only 4 bits toggle in a pause with POW-R
Bit-transparency test: flat EQ at unity must pass identical data; null test should give zero output
Test each DAW software revision for bit transparency
Process at 96 kHz/24-bit and convert to 44.1/16 last
Remaster 16/44.1 sources at a higher rate for about 3 dB less in-band distortion
Jitter: one period of 44.1 kHz is about 22.7 ps; variations of 10 ps can be audible
Clock stability for 20-bit at 44.1 kHz: about 25 ps peak to peak
Use internal sync on A/D (recording) and the D/A as master on playback
Jitter reduction boxes and cables mostly change the monitor clock, not the data
Consoles with asynchronous sample-rate converters can lose stereo stability; about 90% of original quality
Mix analog with the multitrack on internal clock where possible
Using peak meters alone for loudness; peak-only meters do not show program level
Peaking every master to full scale, including low-crest classical and string quartets
Overcompression lowers crest factor and dilutes clarity, impact and depth
Overusing the red zone with a poorly calibrated monitor
Multiple close mics destroy the depth picture
Ignoring mono compatibility after Haas or spread effects
Treating an SPL marking on a monitor dial as meaningful
Confusing gain with level, and monitor gain with monitor SPL
Using peak-only digital meters with no calibrated monitor
Using a jitter-susceptible converter or loose cabling for critical monitoring
Measure bits with a bitscope, distortion with FFT, and run a null test for identity
Spectragram can reveal the dither type used on a CD
Gonger test (sine swept through amplitudes) reveals nonlinear noise and buzz
Metadata: dialnorm sets average level at the decoder; mixlev sets monitor gain to match the producer's SPL
Sample-rate audibility: filter design matters more than raw bandwidth
Jitter must sit near the noise floor to be inaudible, per the author's listening tests.
Framing errors, not jitter, cause most glitches and lock-ups (about 99% per the book).
AES framing mismatch: the 180-degree wordclock phase choice can be about 11 ps at 44.1 kHz.
Framing errors add up along a chain; lock the last processor to external sync if needed.
Jitter: 25 ps at 20 kHz information bandwidth gives about -120 dB.
Doubling sample rate to 88.2 kHz costs 6 dB SNR at equal jitter; 20-bit at 88.2 kHz needs about 12 ps.
Each extra bit requires halving jitter.
J-Test artifacts appear near -132 to -135 dBFS, so low readings may be test artifacts.
A simple reclocking flip-flop only removes jitter if the clock lands inside each bit's acceptance window.
A PLL's output jitter is never better than its intrinsic jitter; use FFT jitter measurements before buying.
Cable: 75 ohm coax for unbalanced, 110 ohm for balanced.
Balanced AES: 2-7 V p-p; unbalanced consumer: at least 0.5 V p-p.
Unbalanced consumer output can be raised to about 2.5 V with a single 75 ohm resistor (book's mod, warns voiding warranty).
Wordclock: standard is about 4 V p-p into 75 ohm; receivers should accept 1-5 V.
Reflections become a concern near 1/4 wavelength: about 20 m (66 ft) at 48 kHz, about 33 ft at 96 kHz.
AES3 cable runs up to 100 m are possible with careful termination (OCR shows "4.8 kHz", likely 48 kHz).
Toslink optical: keep under about 5 m (some receivers 10 m).
Optical test: pull the plug back; at least 1/8 inch margin, preferably 1/4 inch.
Test whether a console locks to an external processor by setting the processor to internal clock.
Tempos vary roughly 80 to 110 BPM; feel is slow and laid-back.
Described as quick (allegro) in tempo terms.
Described as very fast (prestissimo).
Typical club mix runs about 6 to 8 minutes.
Dance follows mathematical repetition in blocks of four bars; an element entering at bar 5, 13 or 15 of a 16-bar loop sounds wrong.
Lead is the focus, so bass stays simple. Bass notes sit on off-beats between the on-beat kicks.
Bass is often funky and moving while the melody stays put (oblique motion).
Melody moves while bass stays constant.
Bass is often very loud and runs alongside the kick, so the two conflict.
12-bit sampler grit is a genre trait.
Sample rate often dropped to 22 or 11 kHz for gritty lo-fi tone.
Self-oscillating filter makes pure sine sub-bass, suited to these genres.
Gentler arrangements than trance; the bar-by-bar map below does not suit them.
Sine wave = fundamental only; used for sub-bass. A sub with no harmonics gives filters nothing to act on.
Low pitch is hard to perceive, so bass samples can be pitched an octave below root without artefacts.
Drive: pushing drums and bass a couple of ticks early makes the track feel like it runs faster.
Shorter 16th-note bass stabs feel more frantic than long notes.
Kick first-beat of bar usually strongest by velocity; later hits vary.
Fix kick/bass clash by sidechaining bass to kick: ratio 3:1, fast attack, medium release.
Short-attack compression on kick removes top click and gives deeper dull thud after makeup gain.
Kick punch comes from speaker cone excursion, tied to kick peak versus rest of the waveform.
Using a rock kick instead of 909 or 808 kicks loses the dynamic edge.
Original dance drum machines gave strictly metronomic grids; 16 PPQN is enough for a bare drum loop.
Intro bars 1 to 16: 4/4 drums only, DJ mix-in.
Bars 16 to 32: extra percussion (hats, snares, claps) completes the drum loop.
First body bars 32 to 48: bass plus drums unchanged. Bars 48 to 64: motif enters with slow low-pass opening.
First drop bars 64 to 72: all percussion except kick removed, filter closed; hats then snares return at about the fourth bar, snare roll.
Second body bars 72 to 88 (crash, new motif), then 88 to 104 (strings and chords added, snare roll in last 4 bars).
Second drop bars 104 to 108 (strings and motif only). Reprise bars 108 to 116: 8-bar snare roll with rising volume and opening filters.
Main body bars 116 to 148, then 148 to 180 (extra snares, panning sweeps).
Outro bars 180 to 196: motifs dropped, filters closing; bars 196 to 212: drums only, last 16 bars for DJ mix-out.
Snare crescendo in build, then drop-back; clubbers expect this pattern.
Filter cut-off opens in builds and closes on drops. Sound gets duller then brighter.
Rising notes feel uplifting; higher pitch means more high frequencies.
Intros and outros kept to drums so DJ can beat-match; dropping the beat disorients dancers.
Human hearing 20 Hz to 20 kHz; teens to about 18 kHz, middle-aged lose above 14 kHz.
3 to 5 kHz sounds louder than other ranges.
Low-pass cut-off at the bottom of the range leaves only the fundamental.
A motif above C4 has many highs and few lows; closing low-pass kills it.
High-pass sweep over a whole mix gives phone/radio sound, then opening gives a fat-up effect.
Three or four motifs together clog the mix; filter cut-offs used so they do not occupy the same space.
Lead sits in same range as voice; sidechain the lead from the vocal to clear the mid range.
Squashing a transient with compression cuts high-frequency content.
Reverb pre-delay keeps transient clear; HF damping and decay time make a sound feel farther or smaller room.
Distortion adds harmonics to a sine so other effects have content.
Starting point for recording: ratio 4:1, 8 to 10 dB gain reduction on loudest parts, fastest attack, release about 500 ms.
GR meter should return to 0 dB between kicks; if it only falls to 2 dB the compressor is jumping in harder than needed.
Short release on a kick-dominated loop causes gain pumping; release must recover before the next kick.
Mix pumping: attack 20 to 30 ms, release 250 ms, low threshold and ratio, about 2 dB reduction on the stereo buss.
Heavy compression with low threshold, high ratio on snare gives the thwack heard in trance, techno and house.
Compression raises average (RMS) level without raising peaks; loudness is judged from average, not kick peaks.
Soft knee starts 3 to 14 dB before threshold; 6 to 9 dB soft knees sound most natural.
Auto-hold in sidechain compressors is usually 40 to 60 ms so the detector ignores bass cycles.
Variable-mu valve units run out of range at about 15 to 20 dB gain reduction.
Limiters: 3 to 6 dB of limiting is a reasonable amount; if already compressed, boost no more than 3 dB.
Look-ahead limiters may use a soft attack of 10 or 20 ms.
Gate release usually 50 to 200 ms; breath-through attack about 100 ms.
Sidechain used to duck leads under vocals and bass under kick.
Heavy-handed compression loses excursion: all content at equal volume gives loud but flat track with weak kick.
Chorus, phaser and flanger thicken and widen sounds; flanging and phasing is a staple of house.
Short delay under 30 ms with low feedback widens and fattens leads or driving bass without audible repeats.
Close sources have narrower, more mono reverb; washing a sound in wide reverb collapses its stereo image.
Out-of-phase signals (180 degrees) cancel; relevant to mono-sum checks.
Pan CC value 64 = centre.
Balanced cables rely on phase-inverted copy cancelling noise.
Dance and pop use deliberately limited dynamic range so they stay in your face.
Loudness is judged by average level; louder always sounds better, so level-match when A/B-ing processing.
Too much limiting gives loud but monotonous result.
CD standard 16-bit, 44.1 kHz; each bit adds about 6 dB of dynamic range. Work at 24-bit, dither down.
Digital clipping is harsh; record as hot as possible without clipping.
Limiter after compressor to catch stray peaks.
Professional level +4 dBu is about 11.8 dB hotter than semi-pro -10 dBV.
Over-quantizing and perfect repetition feel sterile; offset notes a few ticks.
Too many melodies fighting each other; bass made too melodic under a busy lead.
Chord changes on every bass note give manic or sterile sound.
Over-compression kills transient and punch; loud and flat track.
Comparing processing without level matching.
Reverb decay too long on repeated motif turns to mush.
Low recording level then boosting raises noise floor with the signal.
Same detuned waves beating faster than 20 Hz separate into two sounds.
Chord progressions listeners know feel safe; hits mostly use simple three-chord bases.
12 major and 12 minor keys; major vs minor mode changes mood (minor feels more serious).
Closest relative minor of C major is A minor (sixth degree).
Four-note major sevenths sound Latin; minor sevenths sound jazz, so rare in dance.
Groove comes from timing offsets and velocity variation; behind-the-beat = laid back, ahead = nervous or intense.
Swing quantize heavily applied can turn 4/4 into a 3/4 feel.
Drum and bass should be placed first in MIDI priority; MIDI timing error of 12 ms can wreck tight rhythm.
Time-stretch tempo shifts beyond about 25 BPM may add artefacts; pitch shifts beyond 5 or 6 semitones sound unnatural.
