Sampled loops left to the sampler clock may drift by seconds over 5 to 6 minutes; retrigger every couple of bars.
Mix of four-to-the-floor kick with syncopated off-beat parts is core of rhythm.
Reverb RT60 = time to fall 60 dB.
Mixer faders: 0 dB near top; unity gain means no change.
Use one shared reverb on aux send; set effect 100% wet and balance on desk.
Euphoric trance: 4-to-the-floor, range 125-150 BPM, most sit 137-145 BPM; too fast loses danceability.
Simple drums and bass, melodic lead is the focus; long breakdowns, big melodic reprise, snare rolls into reprise.
Percussion kept sparse (no busy congas/bongos) so the lead has room.
Kick and snare mostly stay at max velocity; closed hats carry velocity variation.
Slow laid-back beat, 80-110 BPM.
Beats are sampled breaks, 2-bar repeating loop, sparse kick/snare/hats, not grid-quantized, kick and snare pushed slightly ahead for laid-back feel.
Melodic parts are simple and sit behind the rapper; drums first, vocal next, melody last.
Rap may be 4/4 or 3/4 depending on swing wanted.
Below 120 BPM and laid-back; range 80-120, most 110-120 BPM.
Sub-styles: ambient dub (with bass), conventional (4/4 backbeat), beatless, soundscape (slow pop beat).
Kick may be on every beat, on 2 and 4, on 1 and 3, or sparser; feel comes from kick/snare interplay.
Real instruments (guitar, strings, piano, wind) common; drop-out beats.
Trance kick tight, not boomy; example sine around 90 Hz with falling pitch envelope; too-short decay becomes a blip.
Bass is short simple eighth notes placed off the beat, about an eighth after each kick, so low-frequency energy alternates kick, bass, kick, bass (no gaps, no march feel).
Bass on the beat would leave holes between kick hits; bass avoids competing with kick so little transient needed.
Bass stays mostly mono and gets no wide effects; slight distortion ok to help it cut through.
Kick sine pitch guide: 30-60 Hz hip-hop thud, 50-80 Hz lo-fi, 70-100 Hz club kick; overall 30-100 Hz.
Hip-hop 808-style kick: about 60 Hz sine with fast pitch drop; boomy, little attack click; self-oscillating-filter kick around 40 Hz.
Chill kick deep and boomy, about 40 Hz sine; tight kicks sound urgent.
Long kick tails merge with bass and make muddy bottom end; heavy bass pairs with tight drums, light bass pairs with looser drums.
Deep heavy bass is basically a kick with long decay; sub bass is a pure sine, short decay, maybe small click.
Techno bass short and sharp, with a pitch drop "whump"; often no bass at all.
Trance digital bass is not rich in bottom end so it stays out of the lead's way.
Hip-hop bass: real bass guitar feel, few eighth/quarter notes per bar, pitch moves at most 3-5 semitones, played slightly ahead or behind the beat by 8-10 ticks.
Bass guitar low E is about three octaves below middle C.
Layered basses: one layer low, other high-passed so lows do not clash.
Short transient click on a bass should be under 30 ms.
Melodies, chords and bass loop every 8 bars, with crash or short snare roll at bar 8 end.
Intro: drum loop alone for first 16 bars for DJ mixing.
Then new element at bar 16 (percussion or bass), held 16 or 32 bars; first motif then 16 or 32 bars.
First drop: percussion removed except kick and motif, 4 or sometimes 8 bars.
Return with sliced lead teaser 16 to 32 bars, crash or snare roll or double kick every 4th bar.
Breakdown (pads or filtered lead) 4 to 8 bars, then 4- or 8-bar snare roll build to the reprise.
Full reprise typically 32 bars, sometimes 64, crash every 4th bar; ends with 2-bar snare roll then outro of 16 bars of drum loop.
Elements introduced every 4, 8, 16 or 32 bars; adding at bar 7 sounds wrong.
Snare rolls: 16th notes then 32nd notes with rising velocity; 4- or 8-bar roll before reprise.
Drive trick: shift off-beat kicks/snares or bass a tick or two early.
Little arrangement change: same bars repeat, rapper provides movement; occasional beat drop near end of a bar; cymbal crash about every 4 bars.
Sometimes verse/chorus style; couple of extra snares at bar end make a skip.
Synth lead sits in mid and upper mid range, rich in harmonics; other parts must leave those frequencies.
Motif filter closed down while lead plays, opened when lead is absent; motif and lead cut each other to share space.
Bass guitar and bass tones live roughly 100-300 Hz; a few dB wide cut there stops vocal headphone bass buildup.
Sibilance fix: thin cut around 5-7 kHz; de-essers work 2-16 kHz.
Mic low roll-off kept near 120-150 Hz (170 Hz is thin).
Speech intelligibility centred 2.5-5 kHz.
"Telephone" vocal: band-limit to about 1 kHz-5 kHz.
Cowbell fundamentals about 554 Hz and 830 Hz.
Hi-hats, shakers, cymbals live at the top end; avoid compressing them.
Slow relaxed mastering: mid range cut so lows and highs stand out; aggressive tracks cut bass and hats so mids dominate.
Use a spectrum analyser to see free bands after main groove and lead are placed.
Compress the 4/4 kick alone first: fastest attack, low threshold, high ratio, release long enough that next kick lands near end of release (gives pumping).
Kick plus bass pump compressor: ratio 9:1, attack 5 ms, release about 200 ms, threshold set for at least 3 dB reduction on each kick; shorter release pumps bass more.
Snare compressor: attack slow enough to miss transient and grab decay, then make-up gain.
If vocals present, compress lead with vocal in sidechain so lead ducks.
Fast-attack compression on kick crushes transient for the club kick; slower attack gives hip-hop, big beat, d&b kick.
Drums mostly not compressed (raw); if needed 8:1, fast attack, short release, about 2 dB reduction.
Bass: 4:1, attack 5 ms, release about 150 ms, a couple dB reduction; hip-hop does not pump the low end.
Rap vocal: around 5 dB reduction, 4:1, release about 200 ms; ratio not above 6:1. Recording: 3:1, fast attack.
Loops usually uncompressed; if needed slow attack, medium release, 4:1, about 4-5 dB reduction, avoid pumping.
Vocal recording chain example: 3:1 ratio, fast attack; commercial vocal stack: solid state 4:1 about 4 dB then valve 7:1 about 8 dB.
Crunch trick: two compressors in series, first high ratio with pushed gain for mid distortion (big beat, hip-hop, techno drums).
Compare processed vs bypassed at equal volume; louder always sounds better.
Short staccato sounds read as louder than long ones; fast attack reads louder and nearer.
Gate after reverb tames the tail; used on kicks and leads.
Program kick, snare and bass in mono, centre; width only for lead parts.
Never widen bass; apply bass effects (flanger etc.) in mono.
Synth presets exaggerate stereo; in a full mix this causes a wall of sound.
Keep effects mostly on one wide lead; dry elsewhere for contrast.
Lead reverb as send with 50 ms pre-delay, short tail; delays under 30 ms to thicken.
Vocal width from subtle chorus send (about 80% dry, 20% effect) or double track detuned 2-5 cents each way.
Vocals mono centre; doubled phrases panned left/right for emphasis.
Mono is source of polarity-cancel tricks in recording; stereo samples (loops) are fine if kick centred.
Almost no direct loudness numbers in this section. Distortion/compression cut dynamics; hard distortion effects reduce dynamic range.
Mid scoop for slow mastering vs low-end and hat cut for aggressive tracks.
Raw, gritty: 12-bit and 22 kHz sampling for grit; lo-fi through bit/sample rate reduction.
Aim for clean headroom; recording compressor catches peaks to avoid clipping.
Sounds designed solo then clash in mix; build parts against the full arrangement.
Leaving synth effects (reverb, delay, chorus) on every part smears gaps and reduces impact.
Long drum hits fill gaps and reduce rhythm impact.
Compressing hi-hats and cymbals dulls the top.
Too much overlap of kick tail and bass gives muddy bottom.
Closed hat on same position as open hat causes clash; remove it.
Compressing full loop with budget compressor dulls hats and snares; compress kick only first.
Overly busy bass movement pulls attention from lead.
Strict quantizing and over-processing remove the raw feel.
Too wide stereo spread kills the stereo perspective.
Contrast matters: mix fast and slow attack parts; trance/techno/big beat use fast attack and release on bass, kick, snare; house, d&b, lo-fi, chill use longer bass release (notes almost connected).
Static sounds bore; add movement via LFO or filter; sync LFO to tempo.
Lead notes short (32nd/16th/8th); melody rises across 2-bar groups for uplift.
Tempo-synced modulation keeps arrangement tidy.
Pink noise snares for house/lo-fi/ambient (thicker); white noise for d&b, techno, garage, trance, big beat.
Pitching analogue snare up gives d&b snare; down gives lo-fi snare.
Hat decay length changes perceived speed; short decay feels faster.
Time-stretching 67 BPM loop to 150 BPM adds noise (used deliberately in hip-hop, lo-fi, big beat).
Notes shorter than a quarter make a track feel faster; long attacks feel relaxed.
Vinyl crackle layered to sound sampled.
Any slow, laid-back tempo counts; no fixed arrangement is standard.
Harmony stays close to the bass key; chords stay static and simple.
Pop-style shape used as a template: verse 16 bars, chorus 8, verse 16, chorus 8, verse 16, chorus 8, bridge 1, middle eight 8, double chorus 16.
Always 4/4; range 110 to 140 BPM. Common current values 127 and 137 BPM.
Four-to-the-floor kick, 16th closed hats, open hat on the offbeats, clap or snare on beats 2 and 4.
Snare or clap pushed a few ticks early for drive. Dynamics follow a strong-weak-medium-weak kick pattern.
Often built from sampled loops; many loops are cut and rearranged in a slicer.
Mostly drums and percussion; atonal; tempo 130 to 150 BPM, rarely above.
Loops layered, offset from the beat, and sculpted with EQ and filters rather than melody.
Arrangement stays on one constant level; change comes from filters, EQ and effects, not new melodic parts.
Tempo 100 to 120 BPM for the relaxed feel. Drums often from sampled breaks.
Option: speed loop to 150 to 160 BPM, sample at low rate, play lower in the keyboard range to slow and darken it.
Minor keys; chords static, vocals central, bass simple and often off the beat.
Verse and chorus pattern with 16-bar verses and 8-bar choruses, as in the chill-out template.
Tempo for clubs: the book notes that very fast remixes rarely reach the dance floor.
Remix tempo range: most fall between 120 and 145 BPM.
Intro for club or A&R submissions: main elements should start within the first 20 to 30 seconds; club intros of drums only run 16 or 32 bars.
Kick: 90 Hz sine, positive pitch envelope with fast attack and quick decay. Add a square click layer.
Kick decay should be short with immediate attack to keep kick and bass from blurring.
Kick: 100 Hz sine with positive pitch envelope, immediate attack, medium decay.
Bass: sine body plus saw (brighter) or pulse/square (woodier), detuned 5 or 7 cents.
Bass amp envelope: zero attack, fast decay, short release. Filter follows pitch (positive key follow).
Bass should stay centred in stereo; heavy flanging or phasing smears the low end.
Bass: TB303 style, saw plus square, zero attack, fast decay; velocity drives filter cut-off.
Bass pitch movement is mono with heavy portamento.
Bass: sine plus detuned saw; on/off amp envelope (no attack, no decay, high sustain) for a hum.
Bass should stay within a five-note scale and shift no more than five semitones.
Synth bass: saw, sine and triangle (triangle up one octave), high sustain. Detune sine down from saw for fullness.
Bass moves no more than 3, 5 or 7 semitones; often placed a few ticks before or after the beat.
Bass below 50 Hz cannot be judged on near-field monitors; do not boost below 60 Hz on those.
Roll off below 60 Hz for hi-fi playback; do not boost below 40 Hz for vinyl.
Rough club-play curve: 6 dB at 20 Hz sloping to 0 dB at 90 Hz (theory only).
Sub-bass band is under 50 Hz; most monitors and club systems roll it off.
Kick energy sits around 100 to 200 Hz; the click or transient sits around 1000 to 2500 Hz.
Kick and bass must not hit on the same beat; offset the bass to the offbeat (trance uses the eighth).
Kick attack sits at 3 to 6 kHz; low impact at 40 to 120 Hz.
Build loops from sampled or programmed sections in different combinations, then trigger them live from a sampler to create arrangement.
Map arrangement by listening and marking bar counts and new instrument entries.
Layer 3 to 8 loops, then thin out; move a loop a little early or late.
Use the pop template: 16-bar verse, 8-bar chorus, one-bar bridge, 8-bar middle eight, 16-bar double chorus.
Repeat the first two verses before the chorus; add a motif to the second verse to separate them.
Keep a remix close to 4/4 and a steady tempo; mixed meters or drifting tempo confuse club audiences.
General bands: sub under 50; bass 50 to 250; mud 200 to 800; true mid 800 to 5000; high 5000 to 8000; hi-high 8000 to 20000.
Mud area 200 to 800 causes fatigue; cut here first.
Hi-hats and cymbals: HPF at 300; presence 1 to 6 kHz; brightness 8 to 12 kHz; roll off above 15 kHz.
Snare: HPF at 150; snap 2 to 10 kHz; body 400 Hz to 1 kHz; cut at 400 and 800; boost 8 to 10 kHz.
Toms and congas: shelf below 200; Q half-octave at 300 to 800 for presence.
Synth bass fatten: small boost 60 to 80 Hz, thin Q. Punch 120 to 180; rasp 200 to 300.
Vocals: 400 Hz cut of 2 dB (octave Q) for mud; 10 kHz half-octave boost with de-esser for clarity.
Mid instruments: octave-Q cut of 2 to 3 dB at 400 to 800 Hz and 1 to 5 kHz.
Piano: 50 to 100 weight; 100 to 250 roundness; 250 to 1000 mud; 1000 to 6000 presence; 6000 to 8000 clarity; 8000 to 12000 hiss.
Electric guitar: 100 to 250 body; 250 to 800 mud; 1000 to 6000 cut-through.
Synth leads and pads: 50 to 100 weight; 250 to 800 mud; 1000 to 6000 crunch; 8000 to 12000 brightness.
Mastering mud: cut 180 to 225 Hz; harsh: cut near 1.8 kHz; nasal: cut at 500 Hz.
Mastering bands: 40 to 200 body; 100 to 400 mud; 400 to 1.5k body; 800 to 5k clarity; 5 to 7k sibilance; 3 to 10k presence; 6 to 15k air; 8 to 15k sparkle; 20k and up for a Baxandall-style lift.
Mastering high end: wide cut at 14 kHz if harsh; Baxandall: wide Q at about 20 kHz, 6 to 8 dB.
Vinyl: no boosts above 6 kHz (another passage says 8 kHz); roll off above 15 kHz; roll off below 150 on non-kick parts; roll off kick and bass at 40.

Loop compression: high ratio, low threshold, fast attack, medium release; then noise gate.
Bus compression: ratio 12:1, attack 5 ms, release about 200 ms, threshold 0 dB and lowered until kick and snare show at least 5 dB reduction.
Send-style valve compression: low threshold, high ratio, returned and mixed with dry signal.
Drum loops: very low threshold, ratio about 10:1; compress hard, not for pumping.
